pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Downy mildew on brassica crops is caused by the oomycete (fungal-like organism) Hyaloperonospora parasitica.

type_of_disease.quote: caused by the oomycete (fungal-like organism) Hyaloperonospora parasitica

affected_parts.quote: Downy mildew is a foliar disease ... The curds of cauliflower, broccoli, and cabbage heads can be infected ... grayish or black spots will develop on the stem beneath ... Downy mildew may also parasitize the taproot of turnip and radish ... grows throughout the plant tissue

summary.value: Symptoms on seedlings include discolored lesions on the cotyledons that turn into necrotic spots; on older leaves, small angular light green to yellow lesions appear on the upper leaf surface with gray to white masses of spores ("downy" growth) on the undersurface. Lesions enlarge into irregularly-shaped necrotic patches. Heads/curds show pale brown to gray discoloration; roots may develop dark discolored zones spreading from the crown.
summary.quote: Symptoms on seedlings include discolored lesions on the cotyledons that turn into necrotic spots. Symptoms on older leaves appear as small, angular, light green to yellow lesions on the upper leaf surface. ... On the undersurface of the leaf, gray to white masses of spores will develop ("") growth).

diagnostic_features.value: Small, angular, light green to yellow lesions on the upper leaf surface that enlarge into irregularly-shaped necrotic patches, with gray to white masses of spores ("downy" growth) on the undersurface; grayish-white mycelial growth on the underside of leaf spots during high humidity; curds/heads show pale brown to gray discoloration with grayish or black spots on the stem beneath; taproots of turnip and radish show dark discolored zones spreading from the crown; systemic infections cause internal black streaks and patches in stems and floret branches of broccoli and cauliflower.
diagnostic_features.quote: small, angular, light green to yellow lesions on the upper leaf surface. The lesions enlarge with the development of disease and form irregularly-shaped necrotic patches. On the undersurface of the leaf, gray to white masses of spores will develop ("") growth) ... Pale brown to gray discoloration will appear on the surface of the curd or head, and grayish or black spots will develop on the stem beneath ... dark, discolored zones that spread from the crown into the taproot

value: cold-damaged tissues with subsequent secondary leaf rot
look_alikes.quote: Other foliar diseases such as Alternaria blight, anthracnose, or bacterial leaf spot may be mistaken for downy mildew on brassica crops.

conflicts.note: UC IPM and PNW Handbooks use the older synonym Peronospora parasitica; PNW Handbooks notes '= Hyaloperonospora parasitica'. NC State and UMass use the current accepted name Hyaloperonospora parasitica (or H. brassicae s.l.).
UMass Amherst uses Hyaloperonospora brassicae s.l. as the pathogen name, reflecting a narrower taxonomic treatment of the species complex.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: caused by the fungal pathogen Alternaria brassicicola

type_of_disease.quote: caused by the fungal pathogen Alternaria brassicicola

affected_parts.quote: It affects leaves, and often results in head rot. ... Alternaria can enter farms through infected seeds.

summary.value: Symptoms begin as pin-sized black specks on leaves or stems that enlarge concentrically to form target spot or bull's eye lesions with a yellow halo; black sooty spores can form on the surface during high humidity. Head rot first appears as small brown spots on an otherwise healthy head.
summary.quote: The first symptoms to appear are pin-sized black specks found on the leaf surface or stem. The specks enlarge concentrically, creating a distinct target spot or bull\'s eye lesion with a yellow halo.

diagnostic_features.value: Distinct target spot or bull's eye lesion with concentric rings, a yellow halo, and a necrotic center; lesions visible from both sides of the leaf and can easily tear; black sooty spores produced on the surface during extended periods of high humidity; symptoms typically on older, lower leaves first.
diagnostic_features.quote: The specks enlarge concentrically, creating a distinct target spot or bull\'s eye lesion with a yellow halo. The lesions are visible from both sides of the leaf and the necrotic lesions can easily tear. Severe infections on leaves can cause leaves to fall away from the plant. Black sooty spores are produced on the surface during extended periods of high humidity.

conflicts.alternative_value: Alternaria brassicicola; A. brassicae; A. raphani (multiple species possible)
conflicts.note: UMN Extension notes the disease is potentially caused by three pathogens: Alternaria brassicicola, A. brassicae, and A. raphani. Cornell cites only A. brassicicola. Canonical value reflects the primary pathogen cited by Cornell (higher authority ranking as university extension factsheet with direct attribution).

conflicts.alternative_value: Foliar, Stem (no mention of head or seed)
conflicts.note: Cornell lists only foliar and stem symptoms; UMN Extension additionally notes head rot and seed infection. Canonical value merges both sources for completeness.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: species of Pectobacterium [particularly Pectobacterium carotovorum (previously called Erwinia carotovora)]

type_of_disease.quote: The soft-rot bacterium, Erwinia carotovora subsp. carotovora

affected_parts.quote: Bacterial soft rots damage succulent plant parts such as fruits, tubers, stems and bulbs of plants in nearly every plant family

summary.value: Initially causes water-soaked spots that enlarge, become sunken and soft, with mushy and discolored interior tissues (cream to black), often with seepage and a strong disagreeable odor; broccoli and cauliflower heads become brown and sunken.
summary.quote: Initially, bacterial soft rots cause water-soaked spots. These spots enlarge over time and become sunken and soft. Interior tissues beneath the spots become mushy and discolored, with the discoloration ranging anywhere from cream to black. Seepage from affected areas is common. Soft rots are known for a strong, disagreeable odor that accompanies the breakdown of plant tissue.

diagnostic_features.value: A strong, disagreeable odor accompanying the breakdown of plant tissue, along with mushy interior discoloration ranging from cream to black, seepage from affected areas, and foul-smelling liquid secreted from cracks or other openings.
diagnostic_features.quote: Soft rots are known for a strong, disagreeable odor that accompanies the breakdown of plant tissue.

conflicts.alternative_value: Erwinia carotovora subsp. carotovora (syn. Pectobacterium carotovorum subsp. carotovorum)
conflicts.note: PNW Handbooks uses the older name Erwinia carotovora subsp. carotovora while acknowledging Pectobacterium carotovorum subsp. carotovorum as a synonym. Wisconsin Horticulture and USU use the current accepted name Pectobacterium carotovorum. Canonical value reflects the current accepted nomenclature.

USU Extension notes the disease can be caused by multiple species including Pectobacterium carotovorum and Dickeya dadantii. Other sources cite only Pectobacterium. Canonical value uses the primary, most widely cited species.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris is a bacterium that overwinters in plant refuse for up to 2 years and is carried internally and externally on seed.

type_of_disease.quote: The disease is caused by the seed-borne bacterium Xanthomonas campestris pv. campetris .

affected_parts.quote: The pathogen may move into the petiole and spread up the stem or into the roots and become systemic... Symptoms on root crops may not be visible on foliage, but blackened veins appear in the roots... Its most important means of transmission is on seed

summary.value: Symptoms appear as yellow, V-shaped lesions extending toward the base of the leaf resulting in wilt and necrosis, with blackening of veins within lesions and adjacent areas.
summary.quote: Symptoms can appear at any growth stage as yellow, V-shaped lesions that extend toward the base of the leaf resulting in wilt and necrosis. Blackening of veins within lesions and adjacent areas is a diagnostic feature of this pathogen.

diagnostic_features.value: V-shaped chlorotic area with the base of the V at the leaf midrib; veins in affected areas become dark brown or black and appear as a black net when held up to a strong light source; blackened vascular tissue of the main stem; unilateral stunting of some leaves; bacterial streaming (a stream of white substance exiting plant tissue placed in water) is a good indicator of bacterial infection.
diagnostic_features.quote: creating a V -shaped area with the base of the " V " at the leaf midrib. Veins in these areas become dark brown or black; when the leaf is held up to a strong light source, they show up as a black net. Vascular tissue of the main stem then becomes blackened... Unilateral stunting of some leaves occurs.

look_alikes.quote: Symptoms can appear similar to drought stress, overwatering, or excessive fertilizer application.

conflicts.canonical_value: drought stress, overwatering, excessive fertilizer application, Fusarium wilt, Verticillium wilt
conflicts.alternative_value: drought stress, overwatering, excessive fertilizer application (only)
conflicts.note: UMass lists only drought stress, overwatering, and excessive fertilizer application; NC State additionally lists Fusarium wilt and Verticillium wilt as look-alikes.
